content.speakerNotes: CVA6 is a configurable RISC-V processor code base, not one fixed chip. Its family includes both embedded and application-oriented configurations. To evaluate it, separate three questions: what the core does, which configuration you selected, and what surrounds it in the system. We will compare actual parameter files, follow the main data path, and identify where platform software and verification enter. You can then choose a useful next source without reading the entire repository.

scenes.title: A functional map of the core

content.title: From instructions to architectural state
content.subtitle: Functional groups, not a cycle-accurate pipeline diagram.

cards.label: FRONTEND + DECODE
cards.title: Find and interpret
cards.body: Fetch instructions, choose the next program counter, and decode operations.

cards.label: ISSUE + SCOREBOARD
cards.title: Check readiness
cards.body: Track operands, outstanding instructions and available execution units.

cards.label: EXECUTE + COMMIT
cards.title: Compute, then retire
cards.body: Functional units produce results; commit updates architectural state in order.

cards.label: SUPPORTING LOGIC
cards.title: Memory and control
cards.body: Caches, address translation when enabled, CSR state, exceptions and redirects.

sourceAnchors.title: CVA6 architecture and modules
sourceAnchors.claimSupported: Frontend, decode, issue, execute and commit cooperate with caches, CSR state and control. The diagram is a functional map, not a cycle-accurate six-stage schedule.

sourceAnchors.title: CVA6 issue-stage design
sourceAnchors.claimSupported: Instructions issue in program order, while independent functional units may return results in a different order. The scoreboard tracks outstanding instructions and data.

sourceAnchors.title: CVA6 commit-stage design
sourceAnchors.claimSupported: Commit retires instructions, updates architectural state and handles exceptions.

content.speakerNotes: Read the core as cooperating blocks. The frontend fetches instructions and decode interprets them. Issue checks dependencies and resource availability, while the scoreboard tracks outstanding work. Execution units return results, and commit updates architectural state in order. Caches, control registers and exception handling support this path. Address translation depends on the configuration. These four groups are a reading map, not four pipeline stages or a cycle-accurate timing model.

actions.text: Compare the three source snapshots. CV32A60X has one issue port; CV32A65X enables two. Both are 32-bit configurations without an MMU or supervisor and user modes. The selected 64-bit example enables those facilities, plus atomic and floating-point extensions, but has one issue port. A family name does not determine every feature. These are concrete parameter packages, not an exhaustive product table. Select each configuration and follow its source link to check the values.

scenes.title: In-order does not mean one instruction at a time

content.title: Issue order and completion order differ
content.subtitle: Two independent operations can overlap without out-of-order issue.

columns.label: ILLUSTRATIVE SEQUENCE
columns.title: Load, then independent add
bullets: Load: result may wait for memory.
Independent add: can execute once issued.
The add may return its result first.

columns.label: WHAT THE CORE PRESERVES
columns.title: Program-order issue and retirement
bullets: Dependencies and unit readiness can stall issue.
Commit retires in order, even if results arrive earlier.

anchor.label: WIDTH IS NOT THROUGHPUT
anchor.text: Two issue ports describe an upper issue width, not a promise of two instructions completed every cycle.

sourceAnchors.title: CVA6 issue-stage design
sourceAnchors.claimSupported: Instructions issue in program order, while independent functional units may return results in a different order. The scoreboard tracks outstanding instructions and data.

sourceAnchors.title: Derived configuration
sourceAnchors.claimSupported: SuperscalarEn derives one or two issue ports; issue and commit width are separate quantities.

sourceAnchors.title: CVA6 commit-stage design
sourceAnchors.claimSupported: Commit retires instructions, updates architectural state and handles exceptions.

content.speakerNotes: Consider a load followed by an independent add. If memory is slow, the add may return its result first. That does not make CVA6 an out-of-order-issue processor. The scoreboard tracks each outstanding instruction, and commit preserves architectural order. Dependencies, occupied units and memory delays can all reduce throughput. Likewise, two issue ports are a structural capability, not a guaranteed instruction rate. Keep issue width, result completion and retirement separate when reading performance claims.

scenes.title: A core is not a bootable computer

content.title: What must surround a CVA6 core?
content.subtitle: A conceptual Linux-capable system, not a bill of materials for every configuration.

steps.title: Core

steps.title: Platform

steps.title: Validation

content.takeaway: corev_apu, CVA6 SDK and PULP Cheshire are related entry points, not interchangeable names for CVA6.

sourceAnchors.title: PULP Cheshire host platform
sourceAnchors.locator: README: purpose and Getting Started links
sourceAnchors.claimSupported: A separately maintained Linux-capable host platform built around CVA6, developed in the PULP project.

content.speakerNotes: A core alone cannot boot a complete Linux system. It needs a suitable configuration, memory, interrupts, peripherals and a matching software stack. The CVA6 repository contains an application processing unit environment. The separate CVA6 SDK provides a board-oriented Linux flow. Cheshire is another host platform built around CVA6 in the PULP project. These are related but distinct artifacts. Choose a documented platform and its software together; enabling an MMU is not a complete integration plan.

content.speakerNotes: For capabilities, start in core slash include and read the selected package plus derived parameters. For scheduling and state updates, follow the issue and commit modules with the design documentation. For integration, inspect the application processing unit directory. For tests, start in verification and its smoke regression. Fix a repository revision before comparing files. A useful first task is to explain one parameter and trace its effect, rather than trying to understand every module in one sitting.

content.title: A green result answers a scoped question
content.subtitle: Record enough context to reproduce the claim.

items.title: Revision + configuration
items.body: Which commit and parameter package were tested?

items.title: Environment + tests
items.body: Which simulator, reference model and test selection were used?

items.title: Result + remaining gaps
items.body: Did the run pass, skip or fail? What remains outside its coverage?

content.takeaway: A smoke-test pass is useful evidence. It is not full verification, qualification or a guarantee for your system.

content.speakerNotes: Verification results become useful when their scope is explicit. Record the commit, configuration, simulator and tests. Open the job details rather than relying on a green badge. A smoke regression can expose basic breakage, but passing it does not establish full functional coverage, production qualification or correctness in your own system. The tier CI page is a useful starting point for run evidence. This lesson maps those entry points; it does not claim to have built or qualified the processor.

questions.question: Which statement matches the compared configurations?

options.label: CV32A65X enables two issue ports but no MMU or S/U modes.
The MMU is enabled in both compared 32-bit packages.

questions.analysis: CV32A65X sets SuperscalarEn=1 and disables MMU/S/U. build_config derives two issue ports.

questions.question: You selected a Linux-oriented configuration. What remains?

options.label: Nothing: the CPU RTL is a complete computer.
A compatible platform, boot software and system validation.
Only changing the compiler, regardless of board hardware.

questions.analysis: CPU facilities are necessary but not sufficient: platform integration and matching software are separate work.

questions.question: What does a passing smoke regression establish?

options.label: That the executed tests passed in that recorded environment.
That the implementation meets your frequency and area targets.

questions.analysis: The evidence is limited to the selected commit, configuration, tools and tests; coverage and sign-off need more evidence.

actions.text: Apply the distinctions to three decisions. First, decide which claim about the two embedded configurations matches the parameter files. Second, identify what is still needed after selecting an application-oriented core configuration. Third, decide what a successful smoke regression can establish. Use the source links if necessary. The goal is not to memorise every extension flag, but to connect a technical statement to the configuration, system boundary and evidence that actually support it.

takeaways: Family is not configuration; configuration is not system.
Separate issue width, completion and retirement.
Tie every capability or test claim to a concrete source.
